rows.recognizedQuestion: explain CUDA warps.
rows.answer: A CUDA warp is a group of 32 threads that execute together on an NVIDIA GPU. Threads are organized into blocks, and each block is divided into warps; the GPU schedules instructions at warp granularity, with each thread operating on its own data. If threads within a warp take different branches, the warp executes the different paths with nonparticipating threads masked off, which can reduce efficiency. For good performance, try to keep threads within a warp following similar control flow and accessing consecutive memory locations so their memory requests can be coalesced.

    x = float(x)

It then sends that pair to three distinct replicas and waits for all three acknowledgements before returning v. Every completed write of tag t leaves three replicas storing tags at least t. Every completed read returning tag t establishes the same property through its write-back. Replica tags never decrease, and any two three-replica sets among five replicas intersect.

Within a group of reads returning the same tag, preserve real-time order.

This ordering respects real time:
• A completed write before a read forces the read’s tag to be at least the write’s tag, by quorum intersection.
• A completed read before another read forces nondecreasing returned tags, by the same argument.
• A read completing before a write begins must have a smaller tag: its selected tag came from an already-invoked write, and the single writer assigns increasing tags.

An unfinished write observed by a reader can legally be completed in the history extension and placed before that reader; write-back makes its observed tag durable on a quorum even if the writer never finishes. PostgreSQL repeatable read permits write skew: both transactions can commit, leaving nobody on call. Serializable isolation prevents that outcome, provided serialization failures trigger a retry of the entire transaction with a fresh snapshot.

An exact repeatable-read interleaving is:
1. Initially, Alice and Bob are both on call.
2. Alice’s transaction begins and counts two on-call doctors, establishing its snapshot.
3. Bob’s transaction begins and also counts two, before either update commits.
4. Alice’s transaction sets Alice off call. In its snapshot, Bob remains on call.
5. Bob’s transaction sets Bob off call. In its snapshot, Alice remains on call.
6. Alice commits; Bob commits. The committed state now has both off call.

Updating different rows matters because the writes do not conflict on the same row. PostgreSQL repeatable read prevents certain concurrent same-row updates, but it does not enforce this cross-row invariant merely because both transactions read the same count.

Run this setup once:
```sql
CREATE TABLE doctors (
    name text PRIMARY KEY,
    on_call boolean NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO doctors (name, on_call)
VALUES ('Alice', true), ('Bob', true);
```

Run the following transaction in Alice’s session, and the same transaction with 'Bob' substituted in Bob’s session:
```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;

SELECT count(*) AS on_call_count
FROM doctors
WHERE on_call;

UPDATE doctors
SET on_call = false
WHERE name = 'Alice'
  AND on_call
  AND (SELECT count(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call) > 1;

COMMIT;
```

The UPDATE enforces the decision inside SQL rather than relying on an unchecked application branch. The preliminary SELECT is included to match the stated count-then-update workflow; both statements use the transaction’s snapshot.

If any statement or COMMIT reports SQLSTATE 40001, roll back as needed and retry everything from BEGIN: recount the doctors, reevaluate the condition, perform the conditional update, and attempt COMMIT again. Do not retry only COMMIT or reuse the previous count. The SQL is one transaction attempt; an application retry loop must handle failures and should avoid duplicating external side effects.

For correctness, every serial execution preserves the invariant: an update removes a doctor only when more than one is on call, so at least one remains. PostgreSQL serializable isolation ensures successful participating transactions have an equivalent serial execution; the mutually dependent concurrent removals cannot both successfully commit. After a failed transaction retries following the other’s commit, it sees one on-call doctor and updates zero rows. This guarantee assumes all operations that could remove on-call doctors follow the invariant-preserving protocol, and the initial state has at least one on-call doctor.

PostgreSQL repeatable read permits write skew: both transactions can commit and leave nobody on call. Serializable isolation prevents this outcome, provided all transactions affecting the invariant follow the protocol and serialization failures cause a retry of the entire transaction.

An exact repeatable-read execution:
1. Initially Alice=true and Bob=true.
2. Alice’s transaction begins at REPEATABLE READ and counts two on-call doctors, establishing its snapshot.
3. Bob’s transaction begins at REPEATABLE READ and also counts two, before either update commits.
4. Alice’s transaction sets Alice=false. Its own view now has Alice=false, Bob=true.
5. Bob’s transaction sets Bob=false. Its own view has Alice=true, Bob=false; Alice’s uncommitted change is not visible.
6. Alice’s transaction commits, leaving committed Alice=false, Bob=true.
7. Bob’s transaction commits, leaving committed Alice=false, Bob=false.

They update different rows, so neither encounters a concurrent update of the row it writes. PostgreSQL repeatable read does not prevent the cross-row read/write dependency cycle responsible for this write skew.

Run this setup once:
```sql
CREATE TABLE doctors (
    name text PRIMARY KEY,
    on_call boolean NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO doctors (name, on_call)
VALUES ('Alice', true), ('Bob', true);
```

Run the following transaction in Alice’s session; run the same transaction with 'Bob' in Bob’s session:
```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;

SELECT count(*) AS on_call_count
FROM doctors
WHERE on_call;

UPDATE doctors
SET on_call = false
WHERE name = 'Alice'
  AND on_call
  AND (SELECT count(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call) > 1;

COMMIT;
```

The UPDATE contains the condition itself, so no external branching is required. If any statement or COMMIT reports SQLSTATE 40001, roll back if the transaction is still open, then retry everything from BEGIN through COMMIT in a new transaction: repeat the count, reevaluate the condition, and redo the update. Do not retry only the failed statement or reuse the old count; the application must implement this whole-transaction retry loop, and defer irreversible external side effects until successful commit.

For correctness, every serial execution preserves the invariant: an update takes an on-call doctor off call only when at least two are on call, leaving at least one. PostgreSQL serializable isolation ensures successfully committed transactions are equivalent to a serial execution; it cannot allow both transactions to commit with the observations above. After one succeeds, a retried transaction sees only one on-call doctor and its UPDATE affects zero rows. This proof assumes the initial invariant holds and no other transaction bypasses the protocol by deleting doctors or unconditionally taking them off call.

capturedRowMeasurements.nonFaultProbeScope: Excludes requested transport-fault probes, including unsupported or unconfirmed injections. Does not independently certify every remaining sample as a healthy warm connection.

allFollowupUsefulP95Ms.scope: Missing, incorrect and unverified useful delivery rank after finite correct delivery; missing latency is never replaced with a timeout value.

panelTransitions.scope: Sampled viewport transitions and native/host clock bounds. Upper bounds allow prior text until the first observed clearing/new-generation paint; an unobserved blank paint may make the actual interval shorter. Lower bounds use only observed old-generation paint after acceptance. Not a universal stale-output certificate.

generationProjection.scope: Same-generation final observed lifecycle projection, guarded by generation/context/input hash, response revision and original acceptance time. Uses native events already recorded in the immutable journal. Original canonical question, audio source endpoint, viewport samples and recorder-return rows remain preserved. No different generation chosen, no clock reset, unverified identity remains unchanged.
